body.text: How do you reach Datça from Bodrum by ferry or from Dalaman by road?

Travellers reach Datça either via the 1-hour-45-minute car ferry from Bodrum Castle Port to Körmen Harbour or by driving roughly 160 kilometres (2.5 to 3 hours) from Dalaman Airport (DLM) via Marmaris. Taking the ferry cuts hours of winding highway driving if you are already on the Bodrum Peninsula.

Operated on the Muğla provincial network by [Bodrum Feribot](https://bodrumferibot.com/seferler-bodrum-datca?lang=en), crossings increase to four daily sailings in peak summer (mid-July to late August) and drop to fewer winter departures that can cancel in strong winds. According to the [MUTTAŞ 2026 Bodrum–Datça tariff](https://ulasim.muttas.com.tr/storage/uploads/tarifeler/1786697898_Bodrum-Dat%C3%A7a_Feribotu_2026_Tarifesi.pdf), foot passengers pay 1,000 TL one-way (1,850 TL round-trip) and standard cars pay 3,450 TL one-way. From Körmen port, Datça town centre is a quick 10-minute drive south. If you fly into Dalaman instead, expect a scenic pine-forest road past Balıkaşıran—the narrowest waist of the peninsula—where you need a rental car or private transfer to reach the outer bays comfortably.
Why is Old Datça popular for slow travellers?

Old Datça (Eski Datça) sits three kilometres inland from the modern waterfront, preserving a quiet grid of honey-coloured stone houses, cobbled lanes, and bougainvillea-draped courtyards where cars cannot speed through. As noted by [GoTürkiye](https://goturkiye.com/villages/eski-datca), strict architectural preservation rules have kept high-rise resorts out of the village.

The village's literary reputation grew around the late Turkish poet Can Yücel, who spent his final decade here; while his stone house on Can Yücel Sokak is closed to interior tours, his verses remain painted along nearby garden walls, and [GoTürkiye's Datça guide](https://goturkiye.com/datca/see) highlights the slow café rhythm around Orhan's Coffeehouse. Mornings here start with local thyme honey, green-almond preserves, and strong coffee before the midday heat arrives. Evenings bring low-key courtyard dinners rather than beach-club sound systems—exactly why travellers escaping Bodrum's peak-season noise choose Old Datça as their base.
What can you see at ancient Knidos at sunset?

Perched on Cape Tekir at the extreme western tip of the peninsula, [Knidos Archaeological Site](https://muze.gov.tr/muze-detay?SectionId=KND01&DistId=KND) marks the geographic meeting point of the Aegean and Mediterranean seas. Arriving two hours before sunset gives you soft light over its twin ancient harbours, 5,000-seat lower theatre, terraced agora, and circular Temple of Aphrodite sanctuary.

Knidos was an intellectual powerhouse in the 4th century BC, famous for astronomer Eudoxus, physician Euryphon, and Praxiteles's marble Aphrodite sculpture. Foreign visitors pay €5 entry (verify seasonal closing times on [muze.gov.tr](https://muze.gov.tr/muze-detay?SectionId=KND01&DistId=KND), as gates typically close around sunset or 18:00–20:00 depending on the month). Allow 50 minutes to drive the winding 35-kilometre road out from Datça town, and plan your return drive before full dark if you dislike unlit mountain bends.
Where are the clearest coves on the peninsula?

The peninsula's clearest water lines its southern bays—specifically Palamutbükü, Hayıtbükü, Ovabükü, Kurubük, and Akvaryum—all protected inside the Datça-Bozburun Special Environmental Protection Area documented by the [Turkish Airlines travel guide](https://blog.turkishairlines.com/en/palamutbuku-beaches/). Because most beaches here are smooth pebble rather than fine silt, underwater visibility stays glass-clear even in afternoon breezes.
Keep these local habits in mind when bay-hopping:

items: Pack water shoes: Smooth white pebbles heat up fast by noon and make walking into deeper coves easier.
Respect protection rules: Open fires and wild camping are banned across the Datça-Bozburun protected zone during summer fire season.
Visit in shoulder months: Late May to mid-June and September through early October deliver warm sea temperatures without August parking bottlenecks.
Stock up at Saturday market: Datça town's weekly market is the best place to buy unroasted Datça almonds, wild thyme honey, and olive oil directly from peninsula growers.

faq.q: Do you need a rental car on the Datça Peninsula?
faq.a: Yes, if you want to explore Knidos and the southern coves on your own schedule. Local minibuses (dolmuş) connect Datça centre to Old Datça, Mesudiye (Hayıtbükü/Ovabükü), and Palamutbükü, but service to Knidos is infrequent outside peak summer.

faq.q: Can you take a rental car on the Bodrum–Datça ferry?
faq.a: Yes, the car ferry accepts passenger vehicles, though you should confirm with your rental agency that maritime ferry transit is covered under your insurance policy and book your vehicle slot online in July and August.

faq.q: How many nights should you spend in Datça?
faq.a: Three to four nights is ideal: one day for Old Datça and Kargı Bay, one day for Palamutbükü and Kurubük, and one late afternoon for ancient Knidos plus a boat trip to uninhabited coves.

faq.q: Is the sea cold in Datça?
faq.a: Water on the southern coves warms to a comfortable swimming temperature from late May through October. Because Datça sits at the meeting point of the Aegean and Mediterranean currents, the water stays slightly crisper and fresher than shallow bays near Antalya.

faq.q: Can you visit Knidos by boat instead of driving?
faq.a: Yes. Day boats depart from Palamutbükü and Datça harbour in summer, and gulets sailing between Bodrum and Gökova routinely anchor in Knidos's southern harbour for late-afternoon ruins visits.

Datça town and Old Datça remain lived-in year-round, with mild winters and famous almond blossoms peaking in February. However, many beachfront restaurants in Palamutbükü and Hayıtbükü close from November until April.
